name: CAN Bus Wiring and Termination Check (Resistance)
summary: Find open, shorted or mis-terminated high-speed CAN wiring with resistance measurements at the OBD-II connector, before touching a scope.

requires: OBD-II breakout box, or back-probe pins that fit the DLC without spreading the terminals
Vehicle wiring diagram for the bus you are testing

safety: Ignition OFF, key out. Never measure resistance on a live circuit — the reading will be wrong and you can damage modules.
On vehicles with airbags, disconnect the battery negative and wait at least 10 minutes before probing anywhere near SRS wiring. Never probe a yellow connector.
Do not force probes into DLC terminals. A spread terminal creates the intermittent you will spend the next two hours chasing.
Disconnecting the battery clears learned adaptations and radio/security codes on many vehicles. Know what you are about to lose.

notes: Resistance is this firmware's most trustworthy function — decode is accurate within a few percent on the bench unit.
The low-ohm calibration factor is currently per-device and hardcoded to bench unit #1. Confirm your unit against a known 1% resistor once, then trust it.
Zero your leads first with REL (AUTO button). Lead resistance is a few tenths of an ohm and matters at 60 ohms.
Do NOT use this instrument to check pin 16 for battery voltage — meter DC volts above ~10 V is unreliable in this firmware.

instructions.text: Ignition off, key out. Wait for the bus to sleep — on many vehicles modules stay awake for 30 s to several minutes after the door closes and can bias the bus.
instructions.expect: Interior lights out, no relay clicking, nothing cycling.

instructions.text: Select Resistance with LEFT/RIGHT. Touch the two probe tips together and press AUTO to zero the lead resistance (REL).
instructions.expect: Display settles near 0.00 ohm and the REL indicator is on.

instructions.text: Measure between OBD-II pin 6 (CAN High) and pin 14 (CAN Low).
instructions.expect: Approximately 60 ohms. This is the headline reading.

instructions.text: Measure pin 6 to pin 4 (chassis ground), then pin 14 to pin 4.
instructions.expect: High resistance — typically tens of kilohms to open. A low reading means that line is shorted to ground.

instructions.text: Measure pin 6 to pin 16 (battery positive) and pin 14 to pin 16.
instructions.expect: Open / OL. A low reading means the line is shorted to power, which usually takes the whole bus down.

instructions.text: If step 3 read about 120 ohms, unplug modules one at a time and repeat. You are looking for the segment where the second terminator lives.
instructions.expect: The reading stays at 120 ohms until you disconnect the branch containing the break.

instructions.text: Reconnect everything you disconnected, reconnect the battery, and verify the vehicle starts and the fault behaviour is unchanged before you go further.
instructions.expect: No new faults introduced by your own probing.

measurements.label: CANH-to-CANL termination
measurements.fail: About 120 ohm = one terminator missing or the bus is open between the two terminators. About 40 ohm = an extra terminator, often a wrongly-configured aftermarket or replacement module. OL = open CANH or CANL. Near 0 = CANH shorted to CANL.

measurements.label: CAN High to chassis ground
measurements.fail: A low reading is CAN High shorted to ground — chafed harness, water in a connector, or a failed transceiver.

measurements.label: CAN Low to chassis ground
measurements.fail: A low reading is CAN Low shorted to ground. Same causes.

measurements.label: CAN High to battery positive
measurements.fail: Any continuity here is a short to power. Find it before reconnecting the battery.

knowledge_base.why_60_ohms: ISO 11898-2 high-speed CAN is terminated with a 120 ohm resistor at each physical end of the bus. Measured across the pair with the bus unpowered, those two appear in parallel: 120 || 120 = 60 ohms. Anything else is a wiring or termination fault, and this single reading catches a large fraction of real CAN complaints.
knowledge_base.obd_pinout: OBD-II (SAE J1962) pin 4 = chassis ground, pin 5 = signal ground, pin 6 = CAN High, pin 14 = CAN Low, pin 16 = battery positive (always hot). Pin 1 is manufacturer-defined and on GM is single-wire CAN (GMLAN, 33.3 kbit/s), which has no 60 ohm termination — do not condemn it for reading open.
knowledge_base.not_all_buses_reach_the_dlc: Pins 6 and 14 expose the diagnostic bus only. Many vehicles run several CAN segments behind a gateway module, and a chassis or body bus fault will not show up at the DLC at all. Get the wiring diagram and measure at the segment you actually suspect.
knowledge_base.terminator_location: Terminators are usually inside two modules rather than being discrete resistors — commonly the ECM at one end and the instrument cluster or gateway at the other. Which two is vehicle-specific. This matters when you are hunting a 120 ohm reading: disconnecting a terminating module is itself enough to produce 120 ohms, so verify against the diagram before you condemn wiring.
knowledge_base.why_ohms_before_scope: A resistance measurement gives you an absolute, defensible number. This firmware's scope amplitude is not calibrated yet, so the scope tells you about shape and activity but cannot tell you a voltage. Do the ohm work first; go to the scope only for what ohms cannot see — bit-level signal quality and intermittent bus traffic. See the sibling module automotive/can_bus_waveform.
knowledge_base.common_misread: Measuring with the bus awake. Transceivers bias the lines toward 2.5 V and the meter's test current fights that, giving readings that drift or sit somewhere between 60 and 120 ohms. If the number will not settle, the bus is not asleep.
